Let me try to make it concrete by way of example (and this is just how I see it in the context of programs)- 

Say you're running a server efficiency program within a large co. with x,y,z internal customers, and your goal for the half is to improve overall fleet utilization by 10% through your stakeholder teams developing and rolling out a,b,c features.

Strategy would be:
- Which subset of x,y,z customers are you going to target based on certain criteria and trade-offs (eg: how large is their share of the fleet, what features might be needed to realize those wins, how easy are the customers to work with & what incentives do they have to help you with this program)
- Which customers will you intentionally not prioritize
- How will you sequence development and rollout of a,b,c features, how will you secure resources from extended partner teams (or will you work around things you might need)
- What is your rollout plan, ensuring there are no regressions etc.

Right as you are done with planning (or ideally as you are going through planning) you develop a strategy that goes hand in hand with the goals, and it becomes the input / "marching orders" to different workstreams you operationalize.

I've literally done exactly this at Meta this past half.: setting an aggressive goal for the engineering team of a large efficiency initiative (they wanted to focus mostly on landing features), writing a strategy doc on how we get there, defining the KPIs, identifying service owners that stand to realize the highest efficiency gains, leading the execution of the strategy and I'm pretty close to beating the goals I set.

Hi everyone, it would be great if you can help me with this problem. How can I increase the velocity of a small Dev team I have in a small startup ? How can I help them estimate better so that the tasks are not carried out from sprint to sprint? Thanks in advance.

Sounds like you’re already timeboxing deliverables through sprint (assuming it’s 2 weeks).
Objectively speaking there can be couple of reasons for poor estimation:
1) lack of a good backlog grooming + sprint planning with team participation
2) story points estimation takes time and team learns as they continue the journey. Initially you’ll see the estimation ridiculously off but they’ll get better at it over time 
3) sprint retrospect is important so you discuss, reflect and learn as a team.
Story points are subjective and team dependent too. Usually team finds their story points baseline for a sprint after few months and then you can measure velocity effectively. My 0.02$

Hi @kalpanatpm  I have had similar situation, something that helped 

1) Having a point estimation refresher session to get everyone on team on the same page .
2) As @MindFlayer  having well written user stories with acceptance criteria. 
3) Having  well groomed backlog, to enable Engg team to review user stories before backlog refinement and/or spikes for stories with lots of unknowns .
4) having a baseline of how many SP can be taken on in a sprint based on historical data and setting expectations accordingly .
5) Engaging retro asking the hard questions on why team is impending team progress.
Great suggestions. Thank you @MindFlayer @Vaish
Anyone, please continue to give any suggestions you have on this topic. It’ll help me and may be others as well in this channel

Those are really comprehensive answers.  The one I would add 2 thoughts.
1. Its important to get everyone aligned on the goal.  The engineers need to also want to improve velocity.  I think engineers (as we all would in that position) feel threated/worried by the implications of "needing to improve as a team".  It needs to be clear that this is about making the team improve and doesn't speak at all to individuals.  
2. One tactical thing that I had found a lot of success with was to track "expected completion date (even within sprint)" and "# of times completion date changed".  It took months to build the trust with the team to track them, but it was a great metric to identify problem areas.  By looking at completion date changes, we can identify where unexpected delays were occuring, categorize them and then mitigate them.

Prioritizing to get trust from your team (by accommodating the changes requested by your team on retros as much as possible, bringing more transparency, clarity, alignment of the goals,  and building credibility ) always helps. When the team members provide estimated dates and story points, they feel more ownership to finish their task; if possible, ask them to add 20-30% buffer time for unexpected distractions). Ideally, it will be good practice always to do backlog grooming for the next six sprints, and it helps the entire team visualize what tasks are coming up. Make the team feel appreciated for the work and bring senior leadership visibility to their work. messages.content: How is management interview different than Individual contributor interview? What are the different skills expected for management role than IC role? Leadership questions are also part of Individual Contributor interviews. My understanding is that managers are doing some extra admin work/performance evaluation which is not handled by ICs. Apart from that, all other responsibilities are almost the same.

I'm going to try to say this as gently as I can, so please read this in as kind a tone as possible.

If your understanding is that TPM managers are ICs that "just do some extra admin work and write performance evaluations", I would recommend that you not interview for TPM manager roles. That perspective does not set you up for success as a manager, nor does it set up your directs for success.

You are correct, there are a lot of TPM managers that are doing "player-coach" roles in that they are doing both IC and management work. The "player-coach" model is not ideal, because it means the manager isn't able to focus on the job of management, but it is common. This is incorrectly minimizing how hard the "coach" part is. 

What does a TPM manager do that a TPM IC doesn't? It's the same thing any manager does. I recommend reading "High Output Management" by Andy Grove or "The Effective Manager" by Mark Horstman if you want details on what a manager does. If TPMs are expected to be strategic leaders, TPM managers are expected to lead on yet a higher abstraction layer of strategy. 

Managers are expected to recruit the best talent available to them, develop their current talent to become even more effective, retain their current talent when other companies try to poach them, define when and how TPM ICs should be deployed, triage which programs/areas get the most IC support, and interface more directly with executive leadership and partner leaders. Management can and should be a full-time job.

To more directly answer your question: management questions are pretty straightforward to predict, but hard to answer:
* Describe your management style
* Tell me about a time that you had a deal with an underperforming direct report (including potentially managing them out)
* Tell me about a time that you leveled-up (ideally promoted) a direct report
* Tell me about how you define your TPM team's charter (this can include defining basic roles & responsibilities like ensuring TPMs aren't seen as Jira or calendar admins)
* Tell me about how you set your TPM team's goals to be in line with what the business and organization need
* Tell me about how you ensure your team is effectively performing their duties
* Tell me about how you onboard your new hires to ensure their success
* Tell me about how you delegate tasks to your directs

Recruiting, developing, and retaining talent is an extremely difficult and taxing art to do well. For me, that meant always networking to find top-tier talent willing to leave their current situation to go do something new. Managing meant meeting with my directs every week and asking them "Are you happy, are you bored, how is your work-life balance?" in addition to "how are your programs going?".

 Managing meant proactively thinking about trainings and resources I could provide my team to up-level them (and ideally up-level the org). Managing meant drafting dive-and-save letters to justify compensation increases to fend off FB recruiting trying to poach my top folks. Managing meant angsting about if I should have PIP-ed an employee sooner or been wrong to promote someone a little early. It's real mental and emotional labor that shouldn't be taken lightly.

@staff-tpm I’ve encountered this countless times at Amazon.

I’m not sure that there’s a technical/process solution to the “organizational chaos” phenomenon.

I’m beginning to accept (still find it unpleasant) that there will always be work duplication that leads to churn and inefficiency.

In response, I’ve driven a TPM led Critical Project Review (CPR) mechanism as a weekly office hours which allows anyone to sign up (also TPMs can sign up stakeholders at their discretion). This has shifted our orgs approach from churn prevention to driving progressive convergence relative to customer need by dates.

What I like about our convergence approach is that it  focuses TPM effort towards mature projects. Over time this naturally earns trust with leadership to involve TPMs during bi-annual planning cycles.

I still personally question the efficacy of Amazon’s planning cycles. During my 10 years I’ve seen most of our goals change mid year due to either organizational reshuffling or external forces e.g. COVID, AI etc. The biggest indicator of this are the % of projects with names like {Product} Lite, and launch caveats like “P0.5 fast follow“ during Q4 in last ditch attempts to still “meet” Q1 goals.

Our team’s most effective tool to mitigate wasted effort has been cultivating strong partnerships with our flagship product/UX leaders and carefully curating feature taxonomies which structure user stories and acceptance criteria into no more than two tier hierarchies.

This enabled us to consistently identify intersectional feature similarities and then adjust engineering designs and their respective priorities accordingly. The hierarchical feature pivot table is also an invaluable tool for RAID and SWOT exercises and has become the go to artifact to truly understand the health and vision of each product!

messages.content: Damn, reviewing applications is gonna be time consuming given how many candidates are looking and how easily AI is crawling job boards. Recruiting posted my JD at noon and it's already got 70 applications after only 6 hours
Any tips to try and stand out from the noise?

Most of my advice isn't "tips" per se. 
* The most important thing is to do excellent work on complex problems. 
* The second most important thing is to forge great relationships with people who will vouch for you with their whole chest. 
A referral of "This TPM was amazing and you should be fired if you don't at least look at their resume" is very different than "Yeah, I worked at the same company as this guy and he pinged me on LinkedIn for a referral"

Probably the closest thing I have to a "tip" is what I keep repeating ad nauseum in the #resume-review channel. "Say less".

Don't throw a 4 page resume at someone with 100 resumes on the stack and expect them to hang on to your every word. I'm going to spend the same amount of time or less time reading that 4 page resume as I am a 2 page resume. Focus the resume on your most impressive accomplishments and not a word avalanche of every thing you participated in.
Totally resonate with this.

messages.content: Great write up, reminds me of this article by DoorDash https://careersatdoordash.com/blog/6-principles-for-building-a-world-class-tpm-team/

That's a great doc, thanks for sharing.

 I've now added a bit about TPMs driving through the lens of a strong technical perspective to contribute directly to the program's successful definition and execution rather than just tracking work

Love the doc. Kudos to you for starting this. Some honest feedback from some one who  has been a TPM forever. 

What’s Working Well

The “force multiplier” framing is exactly how senior leaders need to think about TPM value. The PM/EM/TPM distinction is crisp and will prevent most role confusion. Calling out what TPMs do NOT do is gutsy and necessary since most orgs avoid saying it out loud. The FAQ format shows real empathy for the reader’s actual question.

Gaps & What Needs to Be Added

No career ladder or scope levels. There is no distinction between TPM, Sr. TPM, Staff, Principal or senior principal. This is a critical gap for hiring, leveling, and performance conversations.

No TPM assignment or intake process. Who decides a program needs a TPM? Without this, teams either hoard them or never ask.

No success metrics. The doc defines what TPMs do but not how you measure if they are doing it well. OKRs, program health, and stakeholder feedback are all missing.

Stakeholder management is undersold. Executive communication, written narratives, RACI clarity, and escalation frameworks all deserve more depth.

No artifacts defined. What does a TPM actually produce? Charters, RAID logs, decision logs, and launch readiness reviews should be named so people know what good looks like.

Risk management lacks methodology. Identifying and mitigating risk is listed as an objective but there is no framework behind it. Even a lightweight ROAM reference would help.

No ambiguity playbook. The doc says TPMs go deep then step back but never explains how to navigate early stage ambiguity in practice.

Cross functional working norms are absent. Role boundaries are defined but the day to day working model with EMs and PMs is not.

No onboarding guidance. How does a TPM ramp onto an in flight program? First 30, 60, and 90 day expectations deserve to be here.

No coverage of AI and ML complexity. Probabilistic timelines, experiment driven sequencing, and data dependencies
Ran out of text limit, so will stop here.

Thank you for the detailed feedback. I agree that there are a lot of logistical details and specifics missing. These were omitted by design because the audience is executive leadership and senior managers for an org that hasn't really had strong TPMs before

The goal of the doc is to align on the framing of the TPM discipline as more than "status bots". If I don't have that buy-in first, the rest of the details are moot.

Fantastic write up btw but a few comments 
1. I would argue that "TPMs own how the work comes together " vs "TPS own when the work comes together". the EM owns the how. i.e PM is what, EM is the how and TPM is the when - easy digestable bite for the exec team 
2. The moment you put "Communicating upwards, downwards, and sideways to enable timely decisions" I feel like that this is the standard TPM from old school and will become front and center focus with execs with TPMs narrowed down as "Status bots". Rephrase to "Bridging the gap between engineering, product, and leadership to translate technical complexity into actionable insights and strategic decisions
3. Great call out on the "What TPMs do NOT do". These actions are ripe to be replaced by AI and can be considered bookkeeping operations

Thanks for the comments
1. "TPM is the when" is digestible, but feels to me like TPM isn't helping shape the technical direction, which feels limiting to me. I pride myself on nudging the architecture & implementation into the better shape than it would have been were I not there.
2. "Communicating upwards, downwards, and sideways" I'll take a look at this again. I was aiming for brevity here and the suggested rephrase feels verbose. I might invert the cause<->effect to get closer at avoiding the focus on status bots

2nd point in this; EM focus on HOW and WHO (internal to team)
3rd point in this; TPM focus on WHEN & WHO (XFN) ultimately leading to what you mentioned ie how work comes together
